title: Peer tutoring and statistics anxiety: a short pasted report
pages:
Peer tutoring and statistics anxiety: a short pasted report
This report is invented for the Appuscholar test corpus.
Abstract
We asked whether weekly peer tutoring lowers statistics anxiety in second-year psychology students. Forty-two students took part. Anxiety fell more in the tutored group than in the comparison group, and exam marks did not differ.
Method
Forty-two second-year students were recruited from two statistics classes. One class was offered weekly peer tutoring and the other was taught as usual. Anxiety was measured with a 20-item scale before and after eight weeks. The sample size was set by the class lists; no power analysis was done.
Results
The tutored group's anxiety fell more than the comparison group's, t(40) = 2.48, p = .017. Exam marks did not differ, t(40) = 0.84, p = .41. Attendance at tutoring was related to the fall in anxiety, r(19) = .52, p = .016.
References
Kumar, R., & Iyer, S. (2018). Peer learning in statistics classes. Teaching of Psychology in India, 4(2), 33-41. https://doi.org/10.5555/tpi.2018.4.2.33
Shah, M. (2021). Anxiety about numbers. Example Press.

title: Night-time phone use and next-day attention
pages:
Night-time phone use and next-day attention
1. Introduction
Many students keep their phones in bed. Earlier studies linked night-time phone use with shorter sleep, but few measured attention on the next day. We asked whether phone use after midnight predicts slower reaction times the next morning.
2. Method
2.1 Participants
Thirty-six undergraduate students (20 women, 16 men; mean age 19.4 years) took part for course credit. Students who worked night shifts were not included.
2.2) Measures
Phone use was logged by an app for seven nights. Attention was measured each morning with a ten-minute reaction-time task.
1.Procedure
Students installed the app on the first evening and completed the task before their first class on each of the seven mornings.
III. Results
Phone use after midnight predicted slower reaction times, r(34) = .41, p = .013. A one-way ANOVA across three groups of phone use was significant, F(2, 33) = 4.12, p = .025.
IV Discussion
Late phone use went with slower attention the next day. The study cannot say that phone use caused the slowing.
5 References
Lee, H. (2019). Phones in bed. Sleep and Study, 3, 1-9.

title: Reading aloud and word memory in Class 6
pages:
Reading aloud and word memory in Class 6
Introduction
Teachers often ask children to read new words aloud. Earlier studies with adults found a memory gain for words said aloud, called the production effect. We tested whether reading aloud can help children remember

the words a day later better than reading them silently. Twenty-four children from one school took part.
Method
Each child read twenty words aloud and twenty words silently, in a random order. The next day each child wrote down every word they could remember in five minutes.

Results
Children remembered more words read aloud (M = 9.1) than words read silently (M = 7.4), t(23) = 3.05, p = .006.
Discussion
Reading aloud helped memory in this small sample. The study used one school and one list of words, so the result needs repeating in other lessons.

title: Homework time and marks
pages: Students in many schools are asked to do homework every evening, and parents often ask whether more homework leads to better marks. This invented paragraph describes a small study written without any headings, as a student might paste the text of a paper copied from a web page. Two hundred students in Class 9 from four schools kept a diary of the minutes they spent on homework for four weeks. Their mathematics and science marks at the end of the term were taken from school records with the consent of the students and their parents. Students who spent up to an hour a day on homework had higher marks than students who spent almost no time on it. Beyond an hour a day the marks did not rise any further, and students who reported more than three hours a day had slightly lower marks than those who reported one to two hours. The diaries were filled in by the students themselves, so some may have reported more time than they really spent. The schools were all in one city, and the study did not record how difficult the homework was or whether a parent or tutor helped. The authors suggest that schools set a clear limit on daily homework and that teachers check how long their tasks really take. They also point out that a diary kept for four weeks may not show what happens across a whole year, when examinations and holidays change the pattern of work. A later study could ask teachers to record the expected time for each task, compare it with the time the students report, and follow the same students for a full school year. Until then, the safest reading of these results is that a moderate amount of homework goes with better marks, and that very long hours do not seem to help. Readers should also remember that a link of this kind does not show that homework causes the higher marks; students who already do well may simply choose to spend more time on their work, and families who value schoolwork may encourage both homework and other habits that help them do well in their studies.

title: Homework feedback and later marks: a pasted paper with a reference list
pages:
Homework feedback and later marks: a pasted paper with a reference list
Introduction
Written feedback on homework is thought to help learning (Hattie & Timperley, 2007). A DOI quoted in the text, https://doi.org/10.1111/body.12345, is not part of the reference list.
Method
Sixty students in Class 8 received written comments on their homework for one term, and their end-of-term marks were compared with those of sixty students who received ticks only.
Results
Students who received comments gained more marks than students who received ticks, t(118) = 2.20, p = .030.

title: नींद और परीक्षा की चिंता: एक काल्पनिक अध्ययन
pages:
नींद और परीक्षा की चिंता: एक काल्पनिक अध्ययन
यह लेख केवल अभ्यास के लिए लिखा गया है। इसमें दिए गए लोग और आँकड़े वास्तविक नहीं हैं।
परीक्षा से पहले के हफ़्तों में कई विद्यार्थी कम सोते हैं और अधिक चिंता महसूस करते हैं। पहले के अध्ययनों ने नींद और चिंता के बीच संबंध दिखाया है, पर यह नहीं बताया कि पहले क्या आता है। इस अध्ययन में हमने पूछा कि क्या एक सप्ताह तक तय समय पर सोने की आदत परीक्षा की चिंता को कम करती है। चालीस विद्यार्थियों को दो समूहों में बाँटा गया।

एक समूह ने सात दिन तक रोज़ एक तय समय पर सोने की कोशिश की और सोने से एक घंटा पहले फ़ोन बंद रखा। दूसरे समूह ने अपनी सामान्य आदतें जारी रखीं। दोनों समूहों ने सप्ताह से पहले और बाद में चिंता की एक प्रश्नावली भरी। प्रश्नावली में बारह प्रश्न थे और हर प्रश्न का उत्तर एक से पाँच के बीच दिया गया।
दोनों समूहों में बीस-बीस विद्यार्थी थे।
Results
तय समय पर सोने वाले समूह में चिंता अधिक घटी, t(38) = 2.10, p = .042। नींद की गुणवत्ता और चिंता में बदलाव के बीच संबंध कमज़ोर था।
References
शर्मा, र. (2019). नींद और पढ़ाई. शिक्षा पत्रिका, 5(1), 10-18. https://doi.org/10.5555/shiksha.2019.5
Nair, A. (2020). Sleep before examinations. Journal of Student Health, 2, 1-9.

title: STUDY HABITS AND SELF-TESTING
pages:
STUDY HABITS AND SELF-TESTING
ABSTRACT
We asked first-year students how they study for examinations. Most reread their notes; few tested themselves. Students who tested themselves reported higher marks.
INTRODUCTION
Self-testing is one of the best-supported study methods, yet many students prefer rereading. We surveyed students in one university to see how often each method is used.

12
METHODS:
Three hundred and ten first-year students completed an online survey about their study methods in the week before examinations.
RESULTS
Students who tested themselves reported higher marks than students who did not, χ² (1, N = 310) = 9.42, p = .002.
BIBLIOGRAPHY
Dunlosky, J. (2013). Improving students' learning. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4-58. https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100612453266

title: Daily reading time and vocabulary growth in middle school
pages:
Daily reading time and vocabulary growth in middle school
Abstract
We followed one hundred and twenty students in Classes 6 to 8 for one
school year and asked how the minutes they read for pleasure each day
related to the growth of their vocabulary. Students kept a short daily
log, and their vocabulary was tested at the start and the end of the
year. Students who read more each day gained more words.
Introduction
Reading for pleasure is often said to build vocabulary, because books
contain many words that children rarely hear in conversation. Most of
the evidence comes from surveys that ask once how much a child reads,
and such surveys depend on memory and on what children think adults
want to hear. Daily logs are more work for students and teachers, but
they record reading close to the time it happens. Earlier log studies
were short, often a few weeks, and they rarely tested vocabulary at the
start and the end of the same period. They also asked children to note
every book by its title, which many found tiring, and so the question
remains open: does a daily log kept for a whole school year show the
same link between reading and vocabulary that the surveys report?
We expected that it would, and that the link would be stronger for the
younger students, who are still learning many common words.

Method
Students from three schools in one district took part. Each evening they
wrote down the minutes they had spent reading anything they chose, from
comics to novels, and their teachers collected the logs every Friday. A
vocabulary test of sixty words was given in the first and the last week
of the school year. The words were chosen from books written for this age
group, and the test was checked with a small pilot group of thirty other
students before the study began. Scores could range from 0 to 60, and a
second form of the test with different words was used at the end of the
year, so that students could not simply remember the first list. Nine
students moved to other schools during the year and were not included
(their logs were kept but not scored)
so the final sample was one hundred and eleven students.
Results
Minutes of daily reading were related to vocabulary gain, r(109) = .34,
p < .001. The link was stronger in Class 6 than in Class 8, but the
difference between the classes was not significant, F(2, 108) = 1.93,
p = .150.
Discussion
Students who read more each day learned more new words over the year,
and the link was clearest for the youngest students, as we expected. The
logs also showed what the students chose to read. Comics and magazines
made up almost half of the minutes in Class 6 and less than a quarter in
Class 8, where novels and books about science and sport took their place.
Teachers told us that keeping the log changed what some classes did in
the evenings, because students compared their minutes with their friends
and asked each other for books. One student wrote on the last page of his
log that he had never read so many comics in one year, and that his
mother had not believed him until she counted the pile beside his bed!
Because the logs were kept by the students, some minutes may have been
added to please the teachers, and the study cannot say that reading
caused the gain: students who already knew more words may read more.

title: Handwriting and typing in lecture notes
pages:
Handwriting and typing in lecture notes
Method
Students in two lecture courses took notes either by hand on paper or by typing on a laptop for six weeks. The notes were collected after every lecture, so that we could count the words in them and compare them with the slides the lecturer had shown and with a recording of what the lecturer had said. Each student also answered ten shorter questions about the lecture at the end of each week, in the same room, at the same time and under the same rules. The questions asked for facts from the lecture and for ideas that linked two parts of it, and two markers who did not know which group a student
was in scored every answer, agreeing on nine answers out of ten before they discussed all the rest.
Students chose their own way of taking notes in the first week and kept it for the rest of the course.
Results
Handwritten notes held fewer words than typed notes in every week of the study, and they held fewer sentences copied word for word from the slides or from the lecturer. Typed notes were much longer, but most of the extra words were copied, and students who typed often wrote down whole sentences that the lecturer had said without changing a word. On the weekly questions the two groups did equally well on the short questions about facts, while the students who wrote by hand did better on the questions that asked them to link two ideas from the same lecture, a difference that was clearest in the
last two weeks, when the lectures were longest and the slides held the most new words of them all.
Students who typed said that typing was faster, and most of them would type again.

title: Mindfulness breaks and attention in lectures
pages:
Mindfulness breaks and attention in lectures
P. Rao, K. Singh (2022). Journal of Classroom Studies
Abstract
Students attended four weeks of lectures that included a two-minute mindfulness break in the middle, and four weeks of lectures without the break. Attention was rated by the students after each lecture. Ratings were higher in the weeks with the break, t(64) = 2.71, p = .009, and the difference was larger in afternoon lectures.
